title: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Fixed cell size”. Scope: nerve cells and ganglia across animal species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Neuron dimensions and cell counts are measurable and existing neuroanatomical resources support restricted comparisons. Taxonomic selection, missing ganglion totals and uncertain homology prevent resolution of the asserted general law.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across species, measure homologous ganglion-cell volumes and total cell counts per ganglion, then test whether cell size varies narrowly while ganglion cell number rises with species body size. Broad neuron-size scaling or no number-size association would refute the generalization.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Body-size metadata are often missing.

Repositories emphasize selected neurons rather than unbiased cell counts.

Homologous ganglia and neuron classes are difficult to align across phyla.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Soma size and cell number are the variables the claim names, and a large open archive of neuronal morphologies spans many species, including some very large and very small animals. That archive is a biased sample of neuron classes, not a survey of ganglia, so the law as stated for animals in general can be tested only on a restricted and non-random subset. The analysis itself is standard once the subset is defined.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare neuronal soma size and the number of cells per ganglion across species that differ widely in body size. A narrow soma-size range, with fewer cells in smaller species, would support the claim; soma size scaling with body size, or no trend in cell number, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Soma size in a reconstruction archive is not a random sample of ganglion cells, and complete cell counts are a thinner subset.

Reconstructions over-represent mammalian cortex rather than whole ganglia of small invertebrates.

fields.label: Dimension scores
